newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Gunmen kill eight at Iranian centre in Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: Gunmen kill eight at Iranian centre in Pakistan.

text.p: Gunmen attacked an Iranian cultural centre in Pakistan's central province of Punjab on Thursday, killing eight people, including its Iranian director, government officials said.
They said several unidentified gunmen had forced their way into the cultural centre in Multan city, in southern Punjab, at around 1 p.m. (0800 GMT) and started shooting indiscriminately.
A government statement said that, apart from the centre's director Muhammad Ali Rahimi, the seven other people killed were Pakistanis, including a policeman and a civilian guard.
Earlier, police had put the number of dead at seven in this second attack on an Iranian cultural centre in Pakistan in a little over a month.
A statement issued by the Iranian consulate-general in the Punjab capital Lahore blamed unspecified "anti-Islamic agents of world imperialism" for Thursday's attack.
Punjab police chief Mohammad Amin said some people had been arrested but he would not disclose their identity at this stage.

On January 19, a crowd of militants from the Sunni Moslem sect ransacked and burned the Iranian cultural centre in Lahore a day after a bomb blast there killed Zia-ur-Rahman Faruqi, leader of the militant Sipah-i-Sahaba Pakistan (SSP) group.
SSP followers blamed militants from the Shi'ite Moslem sect for the Lahore bombing, which killed 26 people and wounded about 90. Shi'ite groups denied they were involved.

Allama Sajid Naqvi, the Islamabad-based leader of the Shi'ite Tehrik-i-Jafria Pakistan (TJP) group, said SSP activists had carried out Thursday's attack in Multan.There was no immediate comment from the SSP.

Violence between militant groups among Pakistan's majority Sunnis and minority Shi'ites cost at least 170 lives last year. Shi'ites make up about 15 percent of Pakistan's population of over 130 million, but are in the majority in neighbouring Iran.
Local officials said several men posing as Shi'ites had visited Rahimi on Wednesday and asked permission to hold a Moslem celebration in the cultural centre.
The same men arrived there on Thursday in two cars and on two motorcycles, threw hot chili powder into the eyes of a police guard, snatched his rifle and started shooting.
Before escaping, the assailants chanted anti-Shi'ite slogans, police and officials said.
Iranian Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati is expected to visit Pakistan next week to deliver invitations for an Islamic summit conference to be held in Tehran in December.

Velayati, who would be the first foreign minister of an Islamic country to visit Pakistan since Nawaz Sharif was elected prime minister this month, was also expected to discuss regional issues, including Afghanistan and the Kashmir dispute.
Iran has in the past urged the Pakistani government to protect Shi'ites from attacks by what it calls terrorists.
